pedagogy.summary: Partitioning shapes into 2, 3 or 4 equal parts is where children learn that a fraction demands EQUAL parts — equal in AMOUNT (area), not necessarily equal in shape or appearance. The two load-bearing ideas: any-number-of-pieces is not enough (unequal pieces are not halves/thirds/quarters), and two shares that look completely different can still be equal if they cover the same amount. Teach by cutting the same shape more than one way, and by comparing equal-area-but-different-shape pieces, so children judge shares by amount, not by look.
bestPractices: Partition the SAME shape several different ways into the same fraction (a rectangle into quarters by vertical cuts, a 2×2 grid, two diagonals) so no single picture becomes 'the' way
Deliberately show equal-AREA but different-SHAPE pieces and have children verify equality by rearranging/overlaying or counting unit squares
Contrast a correct partition with an unequal one that has the right NUMBER of pieces, forcing the equal-parts criterion open
Move beyond halving to thirds (a circle into three) where children cannot rely on repeated halving
Check equality physically — cut and re-lay pieces, or tile them onto a grid — rather than trusting appearance
keyRepresentations: Rectangle partitioned several ways into the same fraction (multiple valid cuts)
Equal-area different-shape pieces that rearrange onto one another
Faint unit-square grid under a shape for checking equal area
commonMisconceptions: Equal shares must look the same / be congruent — rejects equal-area different-shape pieces as 'not fair'
Any N pieces count as Nths regardless of size (ignores the equal-parts requirement)
A shape can only be partitioned into a fraction one 'proper' way
Judges share size by one dimension (length) rather than area
Thinks halving repeatedly is the only way to make parts, so thirds feel impossible

learn.summary: Children learn that a fraction requires EQUAL parts — equal in AMOUNT (area), not necessarily equal in shape or appearance. Two load-bearing ideas: having the right NUMBER of pieces is not enough (unequal pieces are not halves/thirds/quarters), and two shares that look completely different can still be equal if they cover the same amount. Teach by partitioning the same shape several ways and by comparing equal-area-but-different-shape pieces, so children judge shares by amount, not by look. Thirds (and a circle into three) force children off repeated halving.

activities.title: Cut it, re-lay it: equal amount beats equal look
feedback: If the learner says 'the long one is more/less' by looking: have them cut and re-lay the strip onto the fat piece, so they see equal amount despite different shape.
If the learner calls any four pieces 'quarters' regardless of size: set a correct equal partition beside an unequal four-piece one and recompose/rearrange to show only equal amounts count.
If the learner insists only one 'proper' way makes quarters: show several equal-area-checked quarterings side by side and ask them to invent a new valid one.
When a second and third distinct partition each check out as equal, name this explicitly: many partitions give the same fraction.

For thirds, prompt: how do you know all three are equal? Because the three 120-degree sectors are congruent, you can overlay one onto another; otherwise compare the area each covers rather than judging by appearance.

A faint on-screen grid that tints pieces green only when every piece covers the same area is one optional way to make the equal-area check concrete; counting whole squares works only where piece edges follow the grid, and cutting and rearranging is needed to prove equality of differently shaped pieces whose edges cross grid squares.
activities.rationale: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock; instruction should establish that parts be equal in amount rather than accept any partition. Partitioning shapes into equal parts in different ways is a stated Year 2 expectation. Physically rearranging or tiling equal-area different-shape pieces, and producing several valid partitions, is intended to target the 'must look the same', 'any N pieces', and 'one right way' misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock: children must treat the parts as equal (equal amount), and instruction should establish this rather than accept any partition; the guide addresses accepting approximate drawings only if treated as equal.
Year 2 pupils recognise, find, name and write fractions of shapes and quantities and recognise equivalence, including partitioning shapes into equal parts in different ways.
learnerActions: Partition a square into four parts where the pieces look different — e.g. one long thin strip plus some oddly-shaped bits — but each covers the same amount.
Before checking, predict: is the long thin piece the same amount of the square as a fat corner piece? Say why.

Check equality physically: cut the long strip and lay it over the fat piece to see it rearranges exactly onto it. For pieces whose edges follow a faint underlying grid you can also count the unit squares each covers; for diagonal or irregular pieces use cutting and rearrangement rather than counting, since squares get split.
Decide whether all four pieces are quarters and give the reason (each is the same AMOUNT, one of four equal parts).

Now quarter the SAME shape in a completely different way (e.g. three equally spaced vertical cuts giving four equal strips, then a 2x2 grid, then two diagonals) and argue each piece is still a quarter.

Partition a circle into three equal parts (120-degree slices) and explain how you could check the three parts really are equal (overlay one onto another — they are congruent — or compare the area each covers).
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter means each part is the same amount (area) of the whole, one of four equal parts — the pieces may look different as long as each covers the same amount; and the same shape can be partitioned into the same fraction in many valid ways.

activities.title: Sort the partitions: quarters or not?
feedback: If an equal-area different-shape case is sorted into 'does not': ask how the amounts compare, and suggest rearranging/recomposing the pieces (cut and re-lay), or counting grid-aligned squares, to check before deciding — simply laying differently shaped pieces on top of each other will not make them coincide.
If an unequal four-piece case is sorted into 'shows quarters': point to the four-piece-but-unequal trap — four pieces is not enough, they must each be the same amount.
Praise reasons that mention 'same amount / same area / same number of squares' over reasons that mention how pieces look.
activities.rationale: Categorising partitions as equal vs unequal tests the equal-parts and different-shape criteria cleanly. This is a recognition/classification task: it may check and sharpen the criterion, but it does not by itself let the child construct a partition or physically prove equality, so pair it with hands-on cutting and rearranging rather than using it alone.
sourceClaims: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock: children must treat the parts as equal (equal amount), and instruction should establish this rather than accept any partition; the guide addresses accepting approximate drawings only if treated as equal.
learnerActions: Sort a set of partitioned shapes into 'shows quarters' and 'does not show quarters'.
Include cases that are equal-area but different-shape (these ARE quarters) and cases with four pieces of unequal size (these are NOT quarters).
For each 'does not' card, say what is wrong (pieces are not the same amount).
For each tricky 'is' card where pieces look different, say how you could prove they are equal (cut and rearrange/recompose, or count squares where edges follow the grid).
activities.intendedInsight: Whether a partition shows quarters depends on equal amount, not on the number of pieces or on whether the pieces look alike.

activities.title: Which is the bigger share: a third or a quarter?
feedback: If the learner thinks 'four parts means bigger because there are more': have them overlay a third onto a quarter of an identical shape, both cut the same way (e.g. strips in the same direction), to see the third covers the quarter and sticks out, so it is larger.
Tie the result back to the equal-amount idea: thirds are only thirds if all three cover the same amount, and of the same whole each must therefore be larger than one of four equal parts.

Keep the comparison to identical wholes — this is about which portion of the same shape is larger. (As abstract numbers, fractions remain comparable without a shared whole, but that is not this activity's focus.)
activities.rationale: Comparing a third with a quarter of the same whole is intended to address judging share size by appearance or by piece-count, and reinforces that thirds cannot be reached by repeated halving. Partitioning into equal parts and naming thirds/fourths is within the stated age expectations; the size-ordering of unit fractions is a research-informed extension beyond what the cited sources state directly.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recognise, find, name and write fractions of shapes and quantities and recognise equivalence, including partitioning shapes into equal parts in different ways.
learnerActions: Take two identical shapes; partition one into three equal parts and the other into four equal parts.
Predict which single piece is bigger: one of three equal parts, or one of four equal parts, of the same shape.

Check by overlaying one piece on the other when both wholes are cut the same way (e.g. both into strips the same direction, or both into slices from the centre of a circle) so the larger covers the smaller and sticks out; otherwise compare the area each covers.
State the reasoning: cutting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: For the same whole, one of three equal parts is bigger than one of four equal parts — cutting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller.

constraints: Equal shares must be equal in AMOUNT (area); they need not be congruent or look the same.
Having the right NUMBER of pieces is not sufficient — unequal pieces are not halves/thirds/quarters.
Move beyond halving to thirds so children cannot rely on repeated halving; a circle into three (120-degree shares) is a good non-halving case.

Compare share sizes (e.g. a third vs a quarter) only for identical wholes; this scopes the comparison to represented portions. As numbers, fractions remain comparable without a shared whole, but that is not this activity's focus.

Counting unit squares is a valid equal-area check only where piece edges follow the grid; for diagonal or irregular pieces use cutting and rearrangement, since grid squares get split. Overlay alone proves equality only for congruent pieces; for equal-area pieces of different shape, cut and recompose (or count unit squares if their edges follow the grid).

Sorting/categorisation tasks are recognition: they may check and sharpen the equal-parts criterion but do not let a child physically prove equality by rearranging, so use them alongside hands-on cutting and overlaying, not instead of it.
Physical paper/card cutouts have slight thickness and model the ideal flat figure being partitioned; the lesson is about the 2D area partition they represent, for which thickness is irrelevant.

An on-screen faint unit grid that tints pieces green when areas match is one optional way to make the equal-area check concrete, not a required mechanism — cutting and rearranging pieces works too, and is needed for differently shaped pieces whose edges do not follow the grid.
Static galleries of correct/incorrect partitions can serve as a reference but do not let the child test equality by rearranging pieces; pair them with a hands-on check.
A third spatial dimension is not needed for partitioning 2D shapes; keep the work planar unless there is a specific reason otherwise.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row framed a conversation-only approach as 'poor' and claimed talk 'can't replace' cutting/rearranging, and that a static image or 3D 'cannot' teach the equal-area judgement. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established necessity claims; they are softened here to scoped, observable affordances/limits. Discussion and static references can support this learning, even if hands-on manipulation is particularly well suited to proving equal area.
The 'green only when areas are equal' grid and draggable re-tiling pieces are preserved as an optional illustrative example, not a mandatory mechanism, and whether it was ever tested is unknown.

Geometry self-audit: three equal vertical cuts give four equal strips; a 2x2 grid gives four equal quarters; the two diagonals of a rectangle give four triangles each of area (width x height)/4, i.e. equal-area quarters (congruent only when the shape is a square); three 120-degree slices give equal thirds of a circle. No numerical errors found in the source to correct.

Activity 3's unit-fraction size ordering (a third > a quarter of the same whole) is mathematically correct but not directly stated by either cited source; the attached DfE claim supports only the partitioning-and-naming context in the rationale, so the ordering is flagged as an unvalidated extension.
Terminology note: the base shape is kept as a single 'square/shape' through Activity 1 to avoid the inherited square/rectangle switch; any rectangle works equally for the quartering demonstrations.

assess.poeTask: Show a square quartered into four equal-AREA but different-shaped pieces — one long thin strip, one fat corner piece. Ask the child to predict whether the long thin piece and the fat piece are the SAME amount of the square, and to say why before checking. A child judging by shape predicts 'the long one is more' (or 'less'). Then rearrange — cut the strip and lay it over the fat piece, or count the unit squares under each — to reveal they match. The pre-observation reason (shape-based) is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Cut this rectangle into four equal parts a completely different way from your first. How do you know the new pieces are still quarters?
Here is a circle. Cut it into three equal parts. How could you check the three parts really are equal?
If one piece is tall-and-thin and another is short-and-wide but they cover the same amount, are they equal shares? Why?
Which is a bigger share: one of three equal parts, or one of four equal parts, of the same shape? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Amir is wrong — they ARE quarters, because a quarter means each part is the same AMOUNT (area) of the whole, one of four equal parts; the pieces can look different as long as each covers the same amount. For the rectangle, shows two valid quarterings (e.g. three equal vertical cuts, and a 2×2 grid, or two diagonals) and can argue each piece is a quarter.

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal shares must look the same — rejects equal-area but different-shape pieces as not being quarters
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rearrange/overlay the different-shaped pieces so they tile onto one another; count unit squares under each; establish equal AMOUNT as the test
errorPatterns.distractor: They're not quarters — the pieces are different shapes, so they can't be equal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'not quarters, the pieces are different shapes', judging by appearance rather than amount

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal-parts ignored — any four pieces are called quarters regardless of their sizes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast an equal partition with an unequal one that also has four pieces; check by recomposing; only equal amounts count
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, quarters — there are four pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls an unequally-cut four-piece square 'quarters' because there are four pieces

errorPatterns.pattern: One-right-way — believes a shape can only be partitioned into a fraction a single 'proper' way
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate several valid quarterings side by side, each grid-checked for equal area; have the child invent a new one
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces only one quartering and insists other valid cuts 'aren't real quarters'

responseLevels.gap: Judges equal shares by shape (rejects equal-area different-shape pieces) or calls any four pieces quarters regardless of size.
responseLevels.full: Judges shares by equal AMOUNT not shape, produces two or more different valid partitions (including a circle into thirds), justifies equality by area/recomposition, and rejects an unequal cut with a reason.
responseLevels.partial: Agrees equal parts must be the same size and can quarter a rectangle one standard way, but cannot yet accept different-shaped equal-area pieces as equal, produce a second distinct partition, or reliably make thirds.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a paper square cut into four parts. The parts look different from each other — one is a long strip, the others are smaller shapes — but they all cover the same amount of the square. Amir says these can't be quarters, because the pieces are different shapes. Is Amir right? Say why or why not. Then show me two DIFFERENT ways to cut this rectangle into four equal parts.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who believes equal parts must be congruent judges by shape and says 'not quarters — different shapes'; correct reasoning attends to equal AREA, not look. Producing a SECOND distinct partition further separates 'one right way' thinking from a genuine grasp that many partitions give the same fraction.
